items.followUp: Explain the role of water in the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis.

rubric.why: Identifies what light reactions are and where they occur.
rubric.how: Award for stating that these are light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis occurring in the thylakoid membranes.

rubric.why: Photolysis of water supplies electrons and releases oxygen.
rubric.how: Award for explaining that light energy splits water and oxygen is released.

rubric.why: Electron transfer provides energy for ATP formation.
rubric.how: Award for stating that energized electrons pass along an electron transport chain and their energy is used to make ATP.

rubric.why: NADP accepts electrons and hydrogen to form its reduced form.
rubric.how: Award for stating that NADP is reduced to NADPH.

rubric.why: Names the main products of the light reactions.
rubric.how: Award for summarizing that ATP and NADPH are produced for use in the light-independent reactions, while oxygen is released.

modelAnswer: Light reactions are the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis that occur in the thylakoid membranes of chloroplasts.
Chlorophyll absorbs light energy, which excites electrons.
Light energy splits water into hydrogen ions, electrons and oxygen; oxygen is released.
The energized electrons pass along an electron transport chain, and their energy is used to form ATP by photophosphorylation.
NADP accepts electrons and hydrogen ions and is reduced to NADPH; ATP and NADPH are used in the light-independent reactions.

items.followUp: State two health benefits of eating foods rich in dietary fibre.

rubric.why: Defines dietary fibre as the indigestible part of plant food.
rubric.how: Award for stating that dietary fibre is the indigestible plant material in food.

rubric.why: Gives a suitable example or name for dietary fibre.
rubric.how: Award for naming cellulose or roughage as dietary fibre.

rubric.why: Identifies common dietary sources.
rubric.how: Award for naming suitable sources such as fruits, vegetables, whole grains or cereals.

rubric.why: Explains how fibre supports bowel movement and helps prevent constipation.
rubric.how: Award for explaining that fibre adds bulk or retains water, stimulates peristalsis and helps prevent constipation.

modelAnswer: Dietary fibre, or roughage, is the indigestible part of plant food; cellulose is an example.
Important sources include fruits, vegetables, cereals and whole grains.
Fibre absorbs water and adds bulk to the contents of the intestine.
It stimulates peristalsis, helps food move through the intestine and prevents constipation.

items.followUp: Explain how water moves into the phloem at a source during translocation.

rubric.why: Describes loading sugar into the phloem at the source.
rubric.how: Award for stating that sugar, usually sucrose, is actively loaded from a source into the phloem sieve tubes.

rubric.why: Explains the movement of water into phloem and the rise in pressure.
rubric.how: Award for stating that water enters from the xylem by osmosis, increasing pressure in the phloem.

rubric.why: Identifies the pressure gradient as the force moving phloem sap.
rubric.how: Award for explaining that the pressure difference drives phloem sap from the source towards a sink.

rubric.why: Describes what happens to sugar at the sink.
rubric.how: Award for stating that sugar is unloaded at the sink and is used or stored.

rubric.why: Completes the pressure-flow cycle by describing water return and reduced pressure.
rubric.how: Award for stating that water leaves the phloem and returns to the xylem at the sink, lowering phloem pressure.

modelAnswer: At a source, such as a leaf, sucrose is actively loaded into the phloem sieve tubes.
The increased sugar concentration lowers the water potential in the phloem, so water enters from the xylem by osmosis.
This raises the hydrostatic pressure in the phloem at the source.
The pressure difference drives phloem sap in bulk from the source towards a sink, such as a root or growing region.
At the sink, sugar is unloaded for use or storage; water leaves the phloem and returns to the xylem, reducing pressure there.

items.followUp: Define polymers and give one example of a biological polymer.

rubric.why: States that macromolecules are large molecules.
rubric.how: Award for identifying macromolecules as large molecules, generally with high molecular mass.

rubric.why: Provides a valid example.
rubric.how: Award for giving a correct example such as protein, starch or a nucleic acid.

modelAnswer: Macromolecules are large molecules with high molecular mass found in living organisms.
Examples include proteins, starch and nucleic acids.

items.followUp: Give one example of an organism and describe its habitat.

rubric.why: Defines habitat as the place or environment where an organism lives.
rubric.how: Award for stating that a habitat is the place or environment in which an organism lives.

rubric.why: Shows that a habitat provides conditions or resources for the organism.
rubric.how: Award for explaining that the habitat provides the organism with its needs or suitable living conditions.

modelAnswer: A habitat is the place or environment where an organism lives.
It provides the organism with suitable conditions and resources for its needs.

rubric.why: Identifies the term as a law or principle.
rubric.how: Award for identifying a law or principle as a well-established scientific statement.

rubric.why: Explains that it is supported by repeated testing or observations.
rubric.how: Award for stating that a law or principle is supported by repeated tests, experiments or observations.

modelAnswer: A scientific law or principle is a statement of a scientific fact that has been repeatedly tested and supported by observations or experiments.

items.followUp: State one biological problem that can be investigated by an experiment.

rubric.why: Identifies a biological problem as a question or problem concerning living organisms.
rubric.how: Award for stating that a biological problem is a question about living organisms or biological processes.

rubric.why: Connects the problem with scientific investigation.
rubric.how: Award for stating that it is investigated or solved using the biological method or experimentation.

modelAnswer: A biological problem is a question about living organisms or their processes that can be investigated and solved by the biological method.

items.followUp: What is the function of peptidoglycan in bacteria?

rubric.why: Identifies the main components of peptidoglycan.
rubric.how: Award for stating that peptidoglycan is made of sugars and amino acids.

rubric.why: Identifies where peptidoglycan occurs.
rubric.how: Award for stating that peptidoglycan forms part of the bacterial cell wall.

modelAnswer: Peptidoglycan is a polymer made of sugars and amino acids.
It forms the structural material of the bacterial cell wall.
